close.title: Let’s Build the Way In.
close.sub: IP-extension partnerships · Co-productions with immersive in the plan from day one

a.title:
Old Stories,
New Doors
a.subtitle: What five winters of A Christmas Carol VR taught us about classic IP
a.thesis: Beloved stories need new audiences and new revenue beyond the stage and screen. Live immersive theater is a working model for the audience half, and the right partnership supplies the rest.
a.takeaway: The curtain comes down. The story doesn’t have to.

b.title:
Engine Mastery
× Craft
b.subtitle: Why the studios winning in immersive need both
b.thesis: The companies winning in immersive pair engine mastery with craft: photoreal work that runs on the hardware audiences actually have, built by people who know how to give an audience a role.
b.takeaway: Craft makes them care. Engineering makes sure they can.

pool.title:
Every Beloved Story
Hits the Same Ceiling.
bullets: The run ends. The season closes. The house only has so many seats.
The audience that loves it is getting older, and the next one needs a new way in.
Classic IP needs new audiences and new revenue beyond the stage and the screen.
pool.tags: IP value · Audience development · New revenue
pool.notes: Everyone in this room knows this math. You have a story people love. But a run ends, a release window closes, a theater only has so many seats, and the audience that grew up with the story is getting older. The question isn't whether the story still works. It's where the next audience meets it, and who pays for that meeting. We spent five winters working on that question with one very old story.

pool.title: It Started as a Small Ask
pool.subtitle: Originally produced in association with Actors Theatre of Louisville · 2021
bullets: Actors Theatre of Louisville asked us for production assets: digital characters and some video.
We came back with a bigger idea: a full live production of A Christmas Carol, in VR.
They said yes, then gave us their blessing to remount it every year.
pool.notes: In 2021, Actors Theatre of Louisville, whose stage production was adapted and directed by Robert Barry Fleming, asked us for production assets. Digital characters, some video. Not a VR show. We did the research and came back with a bigger idea: if we're building the sets, the characters and the costumes anyway, why not stage the whole thing, live, in virtual reality? They said yes, and then gave us their blessing to remount it every year. That's the part I want producers to hear: the theater didn't hand off its story. It extended it, with a partner, into a new format.

pool.title: A Christmas Carol VR
pool.subtitle: Live actors. Live audiences. One shared virtual stage.
bullets: Live actors with face and full-body capture perform on the streets of a virtual Victorian London
Fully remote: actors, crew and audience each join from wherever they are
Five holiday seasons, 2021–2025 · The final run, December 2025: 15 performances
pool.notes: Here's what it was. A Christmas Carol, performed live inside virtual reality. Two live actors, Ari Tarr and Debbie Deer, switch between every role, performing in Unreal Engine 5 as MetaHumans, with Quest Pro face tracking, on the streets of a virtual Victorian London, directed for VR by David Gochfeld. It's fully remote: the actors, the crew and the audience are all in different places, and they share one stage. Sixty to seventy-five minutes, a curtain time, a house. We ran it for five holiday seasons, 2021 through 2025. The last run, in December 2025, had fifteen performances, plus a Christmas Eve replay streamathon.
This is the audience's view: not row M of a theater, but inside the room, with the characters. Those little lights are the audience.
pool.alt: Inside A Christmas Carol VR: live-performed characters dance at Fezziwig’s party while the audience, shown as small glowing lights, watches from among them
pool.credit: A Christmas Carol VR 2025 trailer · Agile Lens

pool.title: How Audiences Experienced It
pool.subtitle: Not watching a story. Standing inside one.
bullets: Eye contact: the actor sees you, and plays the scene to you
AI Dickens, a digital host voiced with the lead actor’s permission, welcomes guests before curtain
After the show, a live Q&A with the actors
pool.notes: What did it feel like? Intimate. Scrooge can turn and look you in the eye, because the actor can actually see you. Before curtain, guests are welcomed by AI Dickens, a digital host built with our lead actor's voice, cloned with his permission and paid for, so the human performer can save his energy for the show. And afterwards the actors stay for a live Q&A. The audience isn't watching a recording of a play. They're part of a night that only happens once.

pool.title: What It Proved About Classic IP
bullets: A story audiences already love lowers the barrier to a brand-new format
A live show without a building: the house can be anywhere
The value outlived the run: characters, sets, an AI host and live-performance tools we reuse
pool.notes: So what did five winters prove? One: familiarity is an asset. A story people already love lowers the barrier to trying something new. Two: the house can be anywhere. A live show doesn't need a building, so the audience isn't limited to who can get to one. Three: the value wasn't only the show. The characters, the sets, the AI host and the live-performance pipeline carried into our next projects. And I'll be candid about what it didn't prove on its own: we made work that taught us a lot and still needed a different funding and distribution model. A strong experience needs a partner who understands how its audience finds it.
pool.subtitle: Five winters, three lessons

pool.title:
The Run Ended.
The Performance Didn’t.
pool.subtitle: Our replay and film tools, and a December return
bullets: Performances recorded with their motion capture, cues and spatial audio
Replay from any position, on a scrub timeline: review it like dailies
A cinematographer build shoots new camera coverage of a show that’s already over: see it in our demo area
Back this December: the full live show as a replay, not a video, that audiences join together from headsets. Dates to be announced.
pool.notes: We closed the live run in December 2025, after five seasons. But for this room, here's the part that matters most. We recorded the performances with everything in them: the motion capture, the cues, the spatial audio. You can replay a show from any seat in the house and scrub it like dailies, and a cinematographer build lets a director shoot new coverage of a show that's already over. It's in our demo area today. And this December, Carol comes back as a full replay of the live show, not a video: audiences join it together from headsets, with other audience members, just like before. Dates aren't announced yet. ALEX TO CONFIRM: no dates, venue or tickets for the December replay are announced, so give none on stage. The old fourth bullet (RSC rehearsal R&D and Stage Presence toolkit) moved to the xr-pipeline slide.

pool.title: XR Inside a Normal Film Pipeline
pool.subtitle: The crew uses the headset. The audience gets a normal film.

items.t:
Scout a scanned
location in VR

Try lenses, lights
and blocking at 1:1

Pull stills into
the shot list

Rehearse actors
in the virtual set

pool.notes: Most of you will never sell a ticket to a headset, and you don't have to. Here's XR inside a normal pipeline, where the result is still a film. In pre-production: scout a scanned location from anywhere, put a virtual camera in it, try lenses, lights and blocking at full scale, and pull stills into the shot list. On set: rehearse actors in the virtual space, as we did with the Royal Shakespeare Company, capture performances onto digital humans, and see real-time previs. And in post, because we recorded our Christmas Carol performances as data, not video, a director can shoot new coverage after the show is over. The filled dots are things we've built; the hollow one, XR can do today. The audience never wears a headset. ALEX TO CONFIRM: 'Try lenses, lights and blocking' and 'Pull stills into the shot list' credit the UOXR film kit (grabbable camera with 24-85 mm lenses and masks, monitor, film lights, A/B/C marks, Take still), built on 2026-10-21 and not yet merged: call it a prototype, and make those two dots hollow (al: false) if it is not in the demo area. Scouting cites the RSC's 1:1 Swan scan; capture cites Carol's MetaHumans; post cites the Carol replay and cinematographer builds. 'Real-time previs and virtual sets' is a general XR capability, not an Agile Lens credit.

pool.title: XR as the Product
pool.subtitle: One story, more doors, each built on what only XR does

branches.d:
Actors perform live;
the audience stands inside

The full live show replayed;
attendees join from headsets

Flat video that sells it
on every screen

A taste on any device,
no headset needed

Immersive sections at SXSW, Venice,
Cannes, Tribeca: a second audience

pool.notes: The other door: XR as the product. Take one story, A Christmas Carol. The live VR show is the adaptation: presence, an actor who looks you in the eye, an audience that shares the room. The replay is its second life: this December the show comes back as a full replay of the live performance, not a video, that people join together from headsets. Flat trailers and clips sell it on every screen, and a phone or web teaser gives anyone a taste. And an immersive edition opens a door a flat release can't: the festival circuit. SXSW, Venice, Cannes and Tribeca all program immersive work. That's a second audience and a prestige path for the same story. Carol was a Raindance Immersive nominee last year. ALEX TO CONFIRM: festivals are an opportunity, not a claim; nothing here says Agile Lens screened at or was selected by SXSW, Venice, Cannes or Tribeca, and the only approved festival fact is Raindance Immersive 2025 nominee, Best Immersive Theatre. Add a specific program or past inclusion only if you want to name one. The December replay has no announced dates or tickets: give none. The phone/web teaser is an XR option, not a Carol deliverable.

pool.title: Royal Shakespeare Company
pool.subtitle: Virtual rehearsal tools, developed with the RSC
bullets: Actors rehearse in a 1:1 scan of the Swan Theatre; directors follow along from a laptop
Built with theater people, for theater people: the script stays in your hand, like paper
An R&D grant with XR Network+, 2024–2025: tested with drama students, shown in Stratford
pool.notes: With the Royal Shakespeare Company, Royal Central School and NYU's WLab, through an R&D grant with XR Network+, we developed virtual rehearsal tools: a one-to-one scan of the Swan Theatre in Stratford that actors can rehearse inside, while directors follow from a laptop. We tried every clever way to float a script in space. Every actor wanted the same thing: a script they could hold, and put down on the floor. Respect the craft, and the technology disappears.
pool.alt: Actors in headsets rehearse in a studio while a monitor shows them inside the virtual Swan Theatre; a director follows on a tablet
pool.credit: XR Network+ RSC Challenge 2025 film · Agile Lens

pool.title: Heavenue
pool.bigCaption: The cloud platform we built for live performance in virtual space: it hosted A Christmas Carol’s first season, then the remote audience for The Orchard Off-Broadway, 2022
pool.notes: Because we kept needing it, we built Heavenue: a cloud platform for live performance in virtual space. Its first show was Carol's first season. Then The Orchard, Arlekin Players' Chekhov production, which opened Off-Broadway in June 2022 with Mikhail Baryshnikov and Jessica Hecht: we built the remote experience, so the same performance played to a house and to an audience online at once. It worked well, until we could not find the funding to keep it going. That's part of why I'm here: the work holds up; it needs partners with the audience and the money.

pool.title:
Beautiful Demos Are Easy.
Shipping Them Isn’t.
bullets: Immersive work lives or dies in the gap between the trailer and the headset
Engine mastery: it runs, beautifully, on the hardware audiences actually have
Craft: once they’re inside, they care
pool.notes: Most of you have seen a gorgeous immersive trailer for something that never reached an audience, or reached one and stuttered. That gap is where immersive projects live or die. The companies winning in this space do two things at once. Engine mastery: the work runs, beautifully, on the hardware audiences actually own. And craft: once people are inside, they care. Either one alone isn't enough.

pool.title: We teach the engine we build in
pool.notes: Engine mastery first. I've been an authorized Unreal Engine instructor since 2020: more than 300 classes taught, more than 40 courses written. The people who teach the engine are the people who build your project.

pool.title: Photoreal That Actually Runs
pool.subtitle: Heavy scenes, real hardware
bullets: We optimized photoreal digital humans to run on standalone headsets
That moved A Christmas Carol VR from gaming PCs to headsets audiences already own
Increasing access is worth the work, as long as the artistic vision survives
pool.notes: Here's what engine mastery buys you. We optimized photoreal digital humans to run on standalone headsets, no gaming PC required. In 2024 that moved Christmas Carol onto headsets people already own. Our rule: increasing access is always worth the work, as long as the artistic vision survives the trip.
pool.alt: Close-ups of the live-performed digital humans in A Christmas Carol VR: Scrooge, the Ghost of Christmas Present and Marley
pool.credit: A Christmas Carol VR 2025 trailer · Agile Lens

pool.title: Royal Caribbean · Perfect Day Mexico
pool.bigText:
Nearly 1,000 guests.
Four days at sea.
pool.bigCaption: A hot-air-balloon ride over Perfect Day Mexico, aboard Utopia of the Seas, September 2025 · Standalone headsets, offline, about 10 minutes a ride, run by the client’s volunteers from our operations manual
pool.notes: And it has to run where the audience is. For Royal Caribbean, with Endorphin Partners, we built a hot-air-balloon ride over Perfect Day Mexico on standalone headsets that run offline at sea. Aboard Utopia of the Seas in September 2025, nearly a thousand guests rode it in about four days, about ten minutes a ride, run by the client's own volunteers from the operations manual we wrote. Throughput, reset time and battery plans sound unglamorous. On a ship, they decide how many guests ride.

pool.title:
Craft Is
the Other Half.
pool.tagline: Engine mastery gets the scene running. Craft decides whether anyone cares.
pool.notes: That's engine mastery. Now the other half: craft. Ours comes from theater.

pool.title:
What Kind of Partnerships
Are We Looking For?
pool.tagline: Two kinds. Both start with a story you already own or produce.
pool.notes: Which brings me to the question our moderator asked: what kind of partnerships are we looking for? Two kinds, and both start with a story you already own or produce.

pool.title: 1 · IP-extension partnerships
pool.subtitle: With producers and rights holders
pool.bigText:
Bring the story.
We’ll build the way in.
pool.bigCaption: An immersive edition of a world audiences already love: live, location-based, or at home
pool.notes: First: IP-extension partnerships with producers and rights holders. You bring a story world audiences already love. We design and build the immersive edition: a live performance, a location-based experience, something people take home on a headset. The rights stay yours; the audience gets a new door. That's how Carol began: a theater extending its holiday classic with a partner.

pool.title: 2 · Co-productions from day one
pool.subtitle: Immersive inside the financing and distribution plan
pool.bigText:
In the plan,
not bolted on after.
pool.bigCaption: Budgeted with the production: new windows, new audiences, assets that carry across formats
pool.notes: Second: co-productions where immersive is part of the financing and distribution plan from day one, not bolted on after picture lock. When the immersive edition is in the first budget, the digital sets, characters and performances get built once and used everywhere, and the immersive release becomes another window and another audience, not a marketing afterthought. That's the lesson Carol taught us: the experience was strong; what it needed was a partner with the audience and the distribution plan from the start.

pool.title: How we start
pool.bigText:
One story.
One audience.
One prototype.
pool.bigCaption: A short, paid prototype of a single audience moment, then a production plan you can finance
pool.notes: And we start small. One story, one audience, one prototype: a short, paid prototype of a single moment an audience would have in your world. Then a production plan you can actually finance. Come find us in the demo area today and we'll show you what that moment feels like.
